new_symbol_range_suggestions.Ksi: comparable to or above the upper sampled substrate range; choose so that S**2/Ksi is negligible at low S but becomes comparable to Km + S in the high-substrate regime

derivation_notes: The parent is refined by allowing a second substrate molecule to bind nonproductively at high substrate loading, giving the classical substrate-inhibition denominator term S**2/Ksi while retaining the existing competitive inhibitor occupancy law. This preserves the initial-rate algebraic form and reduces to the parent when Ksi is large or sampled S stays far below Ksi.
change_summary: Changed the assumption that substrate binding only promotes catalysis and never suppresses it at high S. The successor adds classical substrate inhibition, creating extra curvature and possible downturns in v_inh versus S while keeping the inhibitor competition mechanism intact.

assumption_audit.released_assumption: Catalysis exclusively from the substrate-bound enzyme state is treated as having no high-substrate loss of activity beyond ordinary Michaelis saturation.
assumption_audit.mechanism: A second, nonproductive substrate interaction at high substrate concentration causes classical substrate inhibition, reducing the fraction of catalytically competent substrate-bound enzyme without changing the reversible competitive binding of inhibitor at the active site.
assumption_audit.parent_reduction: The successor reduces to the parent in the limit Ksi -> oo, or approximately whenever all sampled substrate concentrations satisfy S << Ksi so that S**2/Ksi is negligible.

response_change.parent_relation: At fixed S and Ki, the parent maps inhibitor concentration to rate through a single substrate-modulated saturating effective inhibitor load, so the I-response has one shared compression form across all substrate levels.
response_change.child_relation: Relax the assumption that substrate leaves catalytic competence unchanged after binding by allowing substrate inhibition at high S, so the rate becomes bell-shaped or more strongly concave in S while competitive inhibitor effects still act through the active-site occupancy term.
response_change.observable_effect: When I is held low or moderate and S is swept from below to above Km, the child can show rate flattening or decline at high S, whereas the parent remains monotonically increasing toward Vmax for every fixed I.

evolution_contract.activation_condition: Observable when substrate is sampled into a high-loading regime beyond the ordinary Michaelis rise, so that an inhibitory substrate-binding effect becomes comparable to catalytic occupancy; strongest at high S with low-to-moderate I where residual activity remains measurable.
evolution_contract.train_hidden_contrast: In training, moderate S sweeps may only show extra flattening relative to Michaelis saturation; in holdout extended to larger S, the same mechanism produces an actual downturn, extending the same substrate-loading effect rather than introducing a new process.
evolution_contract.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the limit of vanishing substrate-inhibition strength or when all sampled S stay well below the substrate-inhibition scale.
evolution_contract.domain_mechanism: classical substrate inhibition superposed on competitive inhibition
evolution_contract.scientific_mechanism: A second, nonproductive substrate interaction at high substrate concentration causes classical substrate inhibition, reducing the fraction of catalytically competent substrate-bound enzyme without changing the reversible competitive binding of inhibitor at the active site.
evolution_contract.difficulty_rationale: This is harder than a coefficient-only correction because the added S**2/Ksi term changes the shape of the scored S-to-rate mapping from structurally monotone to potentially nonmonotone, and it does so while coexisting with the existing S-I coupling inside the inhibitor activity term.
evolution_contract.assumption_before: Catalysis exclusively from the substrate-bound enzyme state is treated as having no high-substrate loss of activity beyond ordinary Michaelis saturation.
evolution_contract.assumption_after: A second substrate can bind nonproductively at high S, lowering catalytic competence and adding classical substrate inhibition on top of competitive inhibition.
evolution_contract.before_fragment: Vmax*S/(Km*(1 + ((I/(Ki + beta*I))*(1 + alpha*I/(Ki + I + S)))) + S)
evolution_contract.after_fragment: Vmax*S/(Km*(1 + ((I/(Ki + beta*I))*(1 + alpha*I/(Ki + I + S)))) + S + S**2/Ksi)
evolution_contract.parent_reduction: The successor reduces to the parent in the limit Ksi -> oo, or approximately whenever all sampled substrate concentrations satisfy S << Ksi so that S**2/Ksi is negligible.
evolution_contract.observable_signature: For fixed Ki and low-to-moderate I, sweeping S from below Km to well above it can produce a bend from rise to flattening or downturn in v_inh; the parent cannot do this because its response to S is monotone increasing for every fixed inhibitor condition. The new effect is strongest when S**2/Ksi becomes comparable to Km*(1 + ((I/(Ki + beta*I))*(1 + alpha*I/(Ki + I + S)))) + S.
evolution_contract.shortcut_blocked: A single parent parameter set cannot reproduce both ordinary low-S ascent and a genuine high-S decline at the same fixed I and Ki, because the parent denominator is affine in S outside the saturating competition modulation and therefore yields a structurally monotone increasing rate with S. Retuning Vmax, Km, alpha, beta, or Ki can shift slope and saturation scale but cannot create the added high-S suppressive curvature or bell-shaped profile.

evolution_plan.activation_condition: Observable when substrate is sampled into a high-loading regime beyond the ordinary Michaelis rise, so that an inhibitory substrate-binding effect becomes comparable to catalytic occupancy; strongest at high S with low-to-moderate I where residual activity remains measurable.
evolution_plan.train_hidden_contrast: In training, moderate S sweeps may only show extra flattening relative to Michaelis saturation; in holdout extended to larger S, the same mechanism produces an actual downturn, extending the same substrate-loading effect rather than introducing a new process.
evolution_plan.continuation_path: Recover the parent law in the limit of vanishing substrate-inhibition strength or when all sampled S stay well below the substrate-inhibition scale.
evolution_plan.gap_statement: The current model assumes every substrate-bound enzyme molecule is equally productive regardless of how large the substrate concentration becomes, so substrate can only oppose inhibitor occupancy and never reduce catalytic throughput on its own.
evolution_plan.baseline_assumption: Catalysis exclusively from the substrate-bound enzyme state is treated as having no high-substrate loss of activity beyond ordinary Michaelis saturation.
evolution_plan.scientific_mechanism: A second, nonproductive substrate interaction at high substrate concentration causes classical substrate inhibition, reducing the fraction of catalytically competent substrate-bound enzyme without changing the reversible competitive binding of inhibitor at the active site.
evolution_plan.rationale: A realistic next refinement is to relax the parent's idealization that substrate only activates catalysis and never inhibits it. Vary S over a range extending from sub-Km to well above Km while holding I fixed at low or moderate values and Ki fixed as sampled. The parent predicts a monotone increase of v_inh with S toward an asymptote for every such condition because substrate only relieves competition and fills the catalytic complex. A child with substrate inhibition instead predicts that after an initial rise, further increases in S can flatten the curve more strongly or decrease the rate, with the contrast most visible when the substrate-inhibition scale lies within or somewhat above the sampled S range. This changes the scored input-to-rate mapping itself, not merely an auxiliary quantity. A single refit of the parent cannot reproduce both ordinary Michaelis-like ascent at low S and a genuine high-S downturn at the same fixed I because its S dependence is structurally monotone. The mechanism is scientifically admissible in initial-rate enzyme assays and remains nonnegative and finite when implemented with a standard inhibitory denominator factor.

selected_embedding_pattern.description: Make one process depend jointly on two declared quantities.

scenario_text: Quantify how a reversible active-site inhibitor changes the initial rate of an enzyme at independently varied substrate and inhibitor concentrations. Substrate and inhibitor compete for mutually exclusive occupancy of the catalytic site, while only substrate-bound enzyme can produce product. The experiment remains in the initial-rate regime so that each concentration pair gives an algebraic response rather than a reaction trajectory.
